items.title: feat(gpu): wait for NVML initialization in agent readiness

labels.name: qa/done
labels.description: QA done before merge and regressions are covered by tests

items.body:
### What does this PR do?

When GPU monitoring is enabled, agent readiness waits until the GPU check's NVML telemetry reports `LastNvmlInitSuccess()`, or five minutes have elapsed since startup registration. Readiness is registered during Fx construction, before the health probe server starts, so delayed autodiscovery cannot briefly report the agent ready before the GPU check is configured.

Fx creates one shared `gpu.Readiness` object and passes it through startup to the GPU check factory. The readiness handle and its original deadline survive check cancellation and reloads without package-global readiness variables. A successful NVML initialization satisfies readiness independently of metric collection results; later NVML failures do not revoke readiness once it has passed.

### Motivation

Include NVML initialization in agent startup readiness while bounding the startup delay. `LastNvmlInitSuccess()` requires an actual successful initialization; the `Unavailable()` reporting flag has a five-minute grace period during which it remains false even if initialization fails.

### Describe how you validated your changes

Passed the GPU core-check, agent run, standalone check command, and common check tests (including the Cluster Agent variant) with the race detector in a Linux arm64 build container:

```sh
bazelisk test --config=gorace --strategy=CcConfigureMakeRule=local \
  //pkg/collector/corechecks/gpu:gpu_test_nvml \
  //cmd/agent/subcommands/run:run_test \
  //pkg/cli/subcommands/check:check_test \
  //pkg/commonchecks:commonchecks_test \
  //pkg/commonchecks:commonchecks_test_dca
```

Tests cover successful initialization with empty collections or collection errors, initialization failure during the reporting grace period followed by recovery, later NVML unavailability, readiness before check configuration, the five-minute fallback without a configured check, and cancellation/reloads through the check factory. The run command test also exercises the disabled-by-default readiness dependency.

### Additional Notes

Uses the existing `health.Once` mechanism; readiness updates follow the existing health polling interval. Validation uses NVML mocks; no hardware GPU test was run.

items.title: Linux NVIDIA monitoring via NVML

labels.name: type:feature
labels.description: Issue: new user-facing capability or enhancement

items.body:
## Summary

Add NVIDIA GPU monitoring support on Linux using NVML, with `nvml-wrapper` as the Rust integration layer.

The initial implementation should focus on establishing a reliable NVIDIA provider and mapping NVML devices to HardwareVisualizer's existing stable GPU identity before expanding the supported metric set.

## Problem

HardwareVisualizer currently supports Linux GPU monitoring primarily through the existing AMD and Intel provider paths.

NVIDIA GPUs are detected as hardware, but NVIDIA-specific live metrics are not currently collected through the Linux GPU sampling pipeline.

As a result, Linux users with NVIDIA GPUs cannot receive the same level of GPU monitoring available on other supported hardware/platform combinations.

This leaves a significant coverage gap for Linux desktop and gaming users.

## Proposed Solution

Introduce an NVIDIA-specific Linux GPU provider backed by NVIDIA Management Library (NVML).

Use [`[nvml-wrapper](https://crates.io/crates/nvml-wrapper)`](https://crates.io/crates/nvml-wrapper) to dynamically access the system-provided NVML library rather than bundling NVIDIA libraries with HardwareVisualizer.

The provider should:

1. Initialize NVML only when NVIDIA GPU metrics are requested.
2. Enumerate available NVIDIA devices.
3. Correlate each NVML device with the GPU identity already exposed by HardwareVisualizer.
4. Return available metrics through the existing GPU monitoring abstractions.
5. Gracefully report unavailable metrics or NVML initialization failures without affecting AMD, Intel, or systems without NVIDIA drivers.

### Initial metrics

The first implementation should investigate support for:

* GPU utilization
* GPU temperature
* Dedicated VRAM usage

The following should only be added in the same issue if they fit the existing metric model cleanly:

* Fan speed
* Board power usage

Do not expand the scope only because NVML exposes additional metrics.

## Stable GPU Identity

Before implementing the full provider, verify that an NVML device can be reliably mapped to HardwareVisualizer's existing Linux GPU identity.

The preferred mapping should use PCI information where possible.

For example:

```text
HardwareVisualizer:
pci:0000:01:00.0

NVML:
domain / bus / device
```

The provider must not rely only on GPU name or enumeration order because those values are not sufficient for stable multi-GPU attribution.

If reliable PCI identity mapping cannot be established, stop after the investigation and document the limitation before integrating the provider into the normal sampling path.

## Architecture

Keep NVIDIA-specific behavior inside the Linux infrastructure/provider layer.

The rest of the Core should continue consuming the existing GPU abstractions without knowing whether a metric came from:

* Linux sysfs / DRM
* NVIDIA NVML
* another platform-specific provider

The implementation should preserve the existing Core / App boundary and must not introduce a Tauri dependency into `hardviz-core`.

## Failure Behavior

NVML availability depends on the installed NVIDIA driver and environment.

Expected failure cases include:

* NVIDIA driver not installed
* NVML shared library unavailable
* no NVIDIA GPU present
* metric unsupported by a particular device
* permission or driver communication failure

These conditions must degrade gracefully.

An NVIDIA provider failure must not prevent other GPU adapters or other hardware metrics from being collected.

Missing readings must remain unavailable rather than being represented as `0`.

## Implementation Notes

Candidate dependency:

```toml
[target.'cfg(target_os = "linux")'.dependencies]
nvml-wrapper = "0.12"
```

Prefer dynamic loading through the system NVIDIA installation.

Do not bundle `libnvidia-ml.so`.

Potential provider location:

```text
core/src/infrastructure/providers/linux/
```

The exact module structure should follow the current Linux GPU provider organization rather than introducing a new abstraction solely for this feature.

## Acceptance Criteria

* [ ] NVIDIA GPUs can be identified and sampled on Linux when NVML is available.
* [ ] NVML devices are correlated with HardwareVisualizer GPU adapters using stable hardware identity, preferably PCI BDF.
* [ ] GPU utilization is exposed through the existing live GPU metrics pipeline.
* [ ] GPU temperature is exposed when supported.
* [ ] Dedicated VRAM usage is exposed when supported.
* [ ] Unsupported individual metrics remain unavailable and are not converted to `0`.
* [ ] Missing NVML / NVIDIA drivers do not affect application startup or non-NVIDIA monitoring.
* [ ] Failure of one NVIDIA adapter does not hide valid data from other adapters.
* [ ] Multi-GPU attribution is covered by focused tests where practical.
* [ ] AMD and Intel Linux GPU behavior remains unchanged.
* [ ] `hardviz-core` remains independent from Tauri.

## Out of Scope

* Bundling NVIDIA drivers or NVML libraries
* CUDA integration
* GPU overclocking or fan control
* Changing the existing GPU identity model unless required to fix an actual identity correctness issue
* Exposing every metric available through NVML
* Windows NVIDIA monitoring changes
* Replacing existing AMD or Intel Linux providers

items.title: feat(monitor): NVML-direct metrics for whole-GPU and MIG pods (v2.11 Monitoring)
items.body:
**What type of PR is this?**
/kind feature

**What this PR does / why we need it:**
HAMi per‑pod GPU metrics depend on libvgpu shared‑memory cache requiring `ld.so.preload` mount. Whole‑card workloads incur unnecessary overhead, and metrics return zero silently with `CUDA_DISABLE_CONTROL=true` or on MIG instances.

This PR adds optional NVML‑direct monitoring (`HAMI_MONITOR_WHOLE_GPU=true`), fetching metrics directly via NVML for containers with full physical GPUs or MIG instances, bypassing shm files.
Device plugin skips `ld.so.preload` mount for whole‑card containers unless `CUDA_DISABLE_CONTROL` is explicitly set by users.

**Which issue(s) this PR fixes:**
Fixes #2222
Fixes #2444

**Special notes for your reviewer:**
Validated on RTX 3080 (10GB, driver 575.64.05, CUDA 12.9), K8s v1.28.8, Docker 26.0.2, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS.

Tested: whole‑card pod (feature on/off), vGPU pod unchanged, mixed multi‑container pod with correct GPU UUID.
Helm chart passed `make verify_chart` for default and `devicePlugin.monitor.monitorWholeGPU=true`.

> ⚠️ Supplement note: MIG logic covered by unit tests, real MIG E2E validation pending community check. Use `vGPUmonitor dry-run whole-gpu` to preview classification without enabling the feature.

**Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?:**
Yes.
- Feature off(default): whole‑card containers no longer inject redundant `ld.so.preload` hook
- Feature on: whole‑card and MIG pods use NVML direct metrics collection

**AI Assistance Disclosure:**
This PR was written with AI assistance. All AI-generated content has been reviewed and verified by the author.

items.title: bug: Backend auto-selection ignores the detected compute capability and defaults new installs to a CUDA 13 build that cannot run on Pascal GPUs

type.name: Bug
type.description: A problem that needs a Fix

items.body:
**Version:** v0.8.4
**OS:** Windows 11 IoT Enterprise LTSC 2024 (10.0.26100)

## Describe the Bug

On a fresh install, Jan selects `win-cuda-13-common_cpus-x64` as the "best available backend" and uses it as the default, **even though Jan's own hardware probe has already recorded that this machine's GPU is compute capability 6.1 (Pascal)**. The CUDA 13 backend is built only for `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES='75;80;86;87;89;120;121'` (per #6979), so it contains no kernel image for sm_61 and every model load dies at startup.

The hardware is not the problem, and neither is the driver. Selecting `win-cuda-12-common_cpus-x64` — already present in the very same dropdown, same version tag `b9967`, same GPU, same model file — works immediately.

### This is not a request to re-add Pascal to the CUDA 13 build

I understand that dropping sm_50–sm_70 from the CUDA 13 binaries is intentional, and that #6979 is closed on that basis. I'm not asking for that to change.

**The defect I'm reporting is in the selection logic:** Jan collects the compute capability, then picks a backend that provably cannot execute on the reported device, with no capability check and no fallback — on the default path, for every fresh install of an affected machine.

## Evidence

### 1. Jan records compute capability 6.1

From `settings.json` → `setting-hardware`, written by Jan's own probe:

```json
"gpus": [{
  "name": "NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080",
  "total_memory": 8192,
  "vendor": "NVIDIA",
  "driver_version": "582.66",
  "nvidia_info": { "index": 0, "compute_capability": "6.1" },
  "vulkan_info": { "index": 0, "device_type": "DiscreteGpu", "api_version": "1.4.312" },
  "activated": false
}]
```

### 2. Selection picks the CUDA 13 build anyway, on the fresh-install path

```
[2026-09-28][16:57:49][tauri_plugin_llamacpp::backend][INFO] Determined best available backend: b9967/win-cuda-13-common_cpus-x64 (Category: "cuda-cu13.0")
[2026-09-28][16:57:49][webview:...][INFO] Initial UI defaults: llamacpp_version='b9967', llamacpp_backend='win-cuda-13-common_cpus-x64'
[2026-09-28][16:57:49][webview:...][INFO] Fresh installation or invalid backend detected, using: b9967/win-cuda-13-common_cpus-x64
```

The GPU is also enumerated correctly at this point, so this isn't a detection failure:

```
Available devices:
  CUDA0: NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080 (8191 MiB, 7185 MiB free)
```

### 3. Model load fails, with a raw CUDA error and no actionable message

```
[59865] 0.02.758.488 E CUDA error: no kernel image is available for execution on the device
[59865] C:\w\llama.cpp\llama.cpp\ggml\src\ggml-cuda\ggml-cuda.cu:104: CUDA error
...
{"code":"INTERNAL_ERROR","details":"exit_code=Some(99)","message":"Model Jan-v3.5-4B-Q4_K_XL failed to load"}
```

The user sees *"GGML backend encountered an error"* in the UI. Nothing in the surfaced message points at the GPU architecture or suggests another backend.

### 4. Same machine, same model, same driver, backend from the same dropdown → works

After switching only the backend preference to `win-cuda-12-common_cpus-x64`:

```
[2026-09-28][17:21:58][webview:...][INFO] Backend b9967/win-cuda-12-common_cpus-x64 dependency verification passed (16 libraries resolved)
...
I slot print_timing: id 0 | task 21 | eval time =  2296.82 ms / 96 tokens (23.93 ms per token, 41.80 tokens per second)
```

No configuration change other than the backend was required. This is a direct A/B: identical driver (582.66), identical model file, identical version tag `b9967` — one backend works, the other cannot launch a single kernel.

## Why this needs a fix rather than a workaround

- **It's the default path, not an edge case.** Every fresh install on a pre-Turing NVIDIA GPU lands on the broken backend before the user has configured anything.
- **A working backend ships in the same release.** `win-cuda-11-common_cpus-x64` and `win-cuda-12-common_cpus-x64` are published as `b9967` assets alongside the CUDA 13 build. No extra download, no extra maintenance.
- **"Auto update engine" re-selects it.** The `best available` logic ranks by CUDA version category only (`Category: "cuda-cu13.0"`) and doesn't consult device capability, so the next engine update can re-select an incompatible build even after a user manually chose a working one.

## Suggested fix

Either of these would resolve it, and either is small:

1. **Filter at selection time** — have `determine best available backend` skip any backend whose supported architecture list excludes the detected `compute_capability`, falling back to the next-highest compatible CUDA build (or Vulkan).
2. **Fail over on launch failure** — if the server exits with a CUDA `no kernel image is available` error during startup, automatically retry with the next compatible backend and surface a message like *"GPU architecture not supported by this backend — switched to X"* instead of `GGML backend encountered an error`.

Option 2 also covers users who already have a stored preference and covers backend/driver combinations that weren't known at install time.

## Additional note (possibly separate)

After setting the stored preference to `win-cuda-12-common_cpus-x64`, the following startup line reports a different backend name:

```
[INFO] Using stored backend preference: b9967/win-avx-cuda-cu12.0-x64
```

while the server that actually gets launched is the `win-cuda-12-common_cpus-x64` one. This looks like a legacy backend-key mapping that may be unrelated to this issue — flagging it in case it's the same code path.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| Jan | v0.8.4 |
| OS | Windows 11 IoT Enterprise LTSC 2024 (10.0.26100) |
| GPU | NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080, 8192 MiB, compute capability 6.1 (Pascal) |
| Driver | 582.66 (nvidia-smi reports CUDA 13.0) |
| llama.cpp | b9967 |
| Model | Jan-v3.5-4B-Q4_K_XL |
| CPU / RAM | i5-4590 / 32 GB |

items.title: feat(runtime): run TRTMC bundles natively on Windows
items.body:
## Background

TRTMC's native runtime, CLI and family loader built and loaded only on ELF platforms. They called `dlopen`/`dladdr` and `/proc/self/exe` directly, CMake passed GCC-only flags and a linker version script, and multi-rank launches required OpenMPI's `mpirun`. As a result, a native Windows workstation with TensorRT or TensorRT-RTX could not run TRTMC bundles. That includes multi-GPU context-parallel runs, which NCCL supports on Windows once `nccl.dll` is built from source.

## Exit Criteria

- The core, the CLI, both backends (TensorRT and TensorRT-RTX) and a family plugin build with MSVC and load at run time on Windows.
- A bundle runs on 1 or 2 GPUs on native Windows. Without `mpirun`, `tools/launch_ranks.py` provides the same OpenMPI rank contract that the family runtimes read on Linux.
- Linux behaviour is unchanged.
- Non-goal: porting any model family. Each family moves to the portable NCCL loader on its own schedule.

## Implementation

- **Platform layer in `trtmc_core`** (`trtmc/runtime/dynamic_library.h`). It is model-agnostic and contains:
  - `LoadLibraryExW`/`GetProcAddress` on Windows and `dlopen`/`dlsym` elsewhere;
  - platform library file names;
  - module and executable path lookup;
  - the shared NCCL library selection: `TRTMC_NCCL_LIBRARY`, else `nccl.dll` or `libnccl.so.2`.
  Load errors name the purpose, the library and the symbol. Windows loader errors add a hint for missing DLLs, missing imports and non-64-bit files. The family loader and the C API's runtime-root lookup use this layer.
- **CMake**:
  - an MSVC block: exported DLL symbols, one output directory for the executable and every DLL (the runtime root), `/EHs` so `extern "C"` plugin entry points may throw, and translation of the GCC warning flags;
  - `TRTMC_FAMILIES` optionally restricts which families are built;
  - the TensorRT-RTX backend finds the versioned Windows import library (`tensorrt_rtx_<major>_<minor>.lib`).
  `conanfile.py` stays free of `requires()`: Windows builds pass their `nlohmann_json` package directory through `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH`.
- **CLI**: `--runtime-cache` expands `{rank}` to `OMPI_COMM_WORLD_RANK`, so each distributed rank keeps its own TensorRT-RTX runtime cache.
- **`tools/launch_ranks.py`** starts N local ranks with:
  - the `OMPI_COMM_WORLD_*` variables and one `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` list;
  - a fresh `TRTMC_NCCL_RENDEZVOUS` file per launch;
  - `mpirun --tag-output`-style rank prefixes.
  When one rank fails, it stops the others.
- **Docs**: `website/docs/features/multi-device.md` covers building `nccl.dll` from the NCCL source on Windows (TCC mode, TensorRT 11.4+ or TensorRT-RTX 1.7.1+, CUDA 13.x or 12.9) and how `TRTMC_NCCL_LIBRARY` and `launch_ranks.py` pick it up.
- The architecture tests accept either NCCL loader form, so families can migrate independently.

### Change categories

- [x] Model or runtime behavior
- [ ] Public API
- [ ] ABI
- [ ] Bundle or artifact format
- [ ] Dependencies
- [ ] Documentation only
- [x] CI or developer tooling

## Validation

### Commands and Results

Run on the head named below; exact commands as listed.

On Linux, run in the CI image (`nvidia/cuda:13.3.0-devel-ubuntu24.04`, TensorRT 11.1.0.106), head `6476420c`:
- Source quality: legal headers, `python -m tools.model_ci validate`, complexity (max CCN 10), and ruff / clang-format on the changed files. All pass.
- `tools/tests` architecture contracts: 298 passed.
- Python unit tests (`-m "not gpu and not trt"`): 1492 passed, 2 skipped.
- Native build (`-DTRTMC_BUILD_TESTS=ON`) plus `ctest --label-exclude gpu`: 240/240 passed on the previous revision of this head. The only later change is a refactor of `windows_error_message`, which is Windows-only code; the stacked head containing it passes 241/241.

On Windows 11 (MSVC 2022, CUDA 13.3, TensorRT-RTX 1.7.1.107):
- Configure and build of this head with `-DTRTMC_FAMILIES=ltx_video` produces `trtmc.exe`, `trtmc_core`, `trtmc_runtime`, `trtmc_c`, both backends and the family DLL.
- The stacked LTX-2.5 PR runs `trtmc.exe` on 1 and 2 GPUs (TCC) through `launch_ranks.py` on this runtime. A CP=2 run uses NCCL built from source as documented.

### Hardware, Environment, and Revisions

- Linux: CI image `nvidia/cuda:13.3.0-devel-ubuntu24.04`, TensorRT 11.1.0.106, Python 3.12, head `6476420c` on `main` `afbb9412`.
- Windows: Windows 11, MSVC 2022 (14.44), CUDA 13.3, TensorRT-RTX 1.7.1.107 (pre-release), NVIDIA driver 610.88, 2x RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (TCC), NCCL 2.32.3 built from source (`v2.32.3-1`).

### Not Run / Remaining Gaps

- The GitHub premerge gate had not run on this head when the description was written.
- Windows with the regular TensorRT backend (only TensorRT-RTX was exercised natively on Windows).
- Windows GPUs in WDDM/MCDM mode (only TCC tested; MCDM has no peer access for NCCL).
- More than 2 ranks with `launch_ranks.py` on Windows.
- Families other than `ltx_video`/`ltx2` were not built on Windows.

## Contributor Self-Review

- [ ] I have completed a self-review of this change.

## Notes For Future Readers

- The stacked PR "feat(ltx2): add the LTX-2.5 text-to-audio-video family" depends on this one. Review this one first.
- Suggested review order:
  1. `core/runtime/primitives/dynamic_library.cpp` and its header;
  2. `CMakeLists.txt`;
  3. `tools/launch_ranks.py` and its tests;
  4. the docs.
- `launch_ranks.py` is for single-host runs where OpenMPI is unavailable. Linux CI and `mpirun` launches are unchanged.
- In a multi-rank Windows run, killing a rank while NCCL kernels are in flight can leave the GPUs busy until a reset. Prefer `ncclCommAbort` on timeouts.

### Risk level

- [ ] Low
- [x] Medium
- [ ] High

Risk rationale: touches the shared native runtime, the family loader and the top-level CMake on every platform; Linux behavior is covered by the unchanged Linux test suite, and the new Windows paths are additive.
